name: PaceKeeper
oneLineDescription: A personal running log app for tracking runs, distance, duration, and pace over time.
whatItIs: PaceKeeper is a personal running log application built with Next.js 14 App Router and TypeScript, backed by PostgreSQL via Supabase. It allows a single authenticated user to log runs (date, distance, duration, optional notes), view their history in reverse chronological order with pagination, edit or delete individual runs, and see a dashboard of all-time and weekly summary statistics. All distances are stored in kilometers and converted for display based on the user's preference (miles or kilometers). The application is web-first and mobile-responsive, with no social features, no GPS integration, no charts, and no external fitness service connections.

stack.name: next
stack.purpose: App Router framework for server components and routing

coreUserFlows: A new user signs up with email and password, is redirected to the dashboard, and sets their preferred distance unit.
An authenticated user fills out the run logging form with date, distance, duration, and optional notes, then submits to save the run.
An authenticated user browses their paginated run history, clicks a run to view its detail page, and edits or deletes it.
An authenticated user views the dashboard to see total runs, total distance, runs this week, and distance this week.
outOfScope: Heart rate or other fitness device metrics

dataModel.purpose: Stores authenticated user accounts managed by Supabase Auth.
Stores each user's preferred distance unit (miles or kilometers), defaulting to miles.
Stores each logged run with date, distance in kilometers, duration in seconds, and optional notes.

crossCuttingPrinciples: All run data is private to the owning user; row-level security is enforced at the database layer.
Server Components are used by default; Client Components are only introduced where interactivity requires them.
All data mutations are performed via Server Actions.
Distances are always stored in kilometers and converted to the user's preferred unit only at the display layer.
Durations are always stored in total seconds and formatted for display.
The user's distance unit preference applies globally to all data entry and display across every feature.
Unauthenticated users are redirected to the landing page; authenticated users are redirected to the dashboard.
Semantic HTML, keyboard navigation, associated form labels, and WCAG AA color contrast are required throughout.
specSummary: PaceKeeper is a focused, single-user running log web application. Its purpose is to let a runner record workouts and observe their history over time — nothing more. The technical foundation is Next.js 14 with the App Router, TypeScript in strict mode, Supabase for PostgreSQL and authentication, Tailwind CSS for styling, and deployment on Vercel. Authentication is email/password only with no OAuth, no password reset, and no email verification. Once logged in, a user lands on a dashboard showing four summary statistics: total runs, total distance, runs this week, and distance this week (week defined as Monday–Sunday). From the dashboard the user can navigate to log a new run via a form that accepts date (defaulting to today, rejecting future dates), distance with a unit selector, duration split into hours/minutes/seconds, and optional free-text notes up to 500 characters. Pace is derived automatically. The run history page lists runs in reverse chronological order, paginated at 10 per page, with each row showing date, distance, duration, pace, and truncated notes. Clicking a run opens a detail view where the user can edit any field using the same validation rules as creation, or permanently delete the run after a confirmation dialog. A single user preference — distance unit (miles or kilometers, defaulting to miles) — controls all display and entry throughout the application. All distances are stored internally in kilometers; all durations are stored in seconds. Row-level security at the database layer ensures users cannot access each other's data. There are no charts, no social features, no GPS, no import/export, and no bulk operations.
